author: Horace
title: A ship, a crossing and a bee
about: Three passages from the *Odes*, each in Horace’s Latin and in John Conington’s English verse, first published in 1863. In the first the poet calls to a ship that fresh waves are about to carry back out to sea. The second comes from a poem that begins with a prayer to the ship carrying Virgil to Attica, in Greece. The third is about writing poems: Horace addresses Iulus Antonius, Mark Antony’s son and himself a poet, first on the Greek poet Pindar and then on his own songs.

view.says: Auden quotes the start of the first passage and all of the second early in his book on the sea in Romantic writing, where he describes the attitude that came before. In it the sea stands for disorder, so the ship of state is a figure used only when society is in danger, and a ship belongs in port. To try to cross the sea is rash, close to hubris.
view.quote: to try to cross it betrays a rashness bordering on hubris
view.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 6–7 and 9

lenses.label: Measure
lenses.meterName: long and short syllables in a fixed order: two lines of twelve, one of seven, one of eight
lenses.caption: Under each syllable a dash marks a long one and a curve a short one. A long syllable takes longer to say, and counts as two short ones. Latin verse is measured by that pattern. Auden, writing with Chester Kallman, set two systems apart: Greek and Latin verse count syllables as long or short, English verse as accented or unaccented. The dots are the accents of the Latin words, and they fall on long and short syllables alike. Each twelve-syllable line breaks after its sixth syllable. In the second line a sentence stops at the break: the cry to the ship, asking what it is doing, ends one half, and the command, bravely seize, fills the other.
lenses.why: The measure is made of the lengths of syllables, a long one counted as two short; the break in the middle of the long line lets a question end one half and a command fill the other.

points.say: This adjective means *new*. Its noun, the waves, is the first word of the next line, and the two together are the subject of the verb that stands before the break.
The question to the ship, about what it is doing, runs up to the break. After the break come an adverb, *bravely*, and a command, *seize*.
The harbor, the thing to be seized, is kept for the head of the third line, and the sentence ends on it.

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. What a long syllable is, the lines of this stanza, the break in the long line and the rule of the Latin accent: Allen and Greenough, *New Latin Grammar*, sections 12, 607, 608, 611, 625 and 626. Auden and Kallman on the two ways of measuring verse: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 485.

lenses.label: Allegory
lenses.name: allegory
lenses.plain: one thing presented in the words and another in the meaning, usually by a run of metaphors (Quintilian’s definition)
lenses.caption: Three words are marked: the ship spoken to (navis), the waves (fluctus) and the harbor (portum). None of the ode’s twenty lines names Rome. Quintilian, who taught rhetoric there, quotes the opening, as far as the harbor, as his example of allegory: ship for the state, waves and storms for civil wars, harbor for peace and concord. Cicero has a ship of the commonwealth tossing in storms of discord, and the edition printed here says the ode seems a close imitation of one the Greek poet Alcaeus wrote during the troubles of his own city, Mitylene. Auden quotes the same opening. The metaphor, he wrote, is used only when society is in danger, and a ship belongs in port.
lenses.why: The ode never names what the ship is; Quintilian reads ship, waves and harbor as the state, civil wars and peace, and Auden says writers bring in the ship of state only when society is in danger.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and [the whole ode](#/read/horace-la/o1-14:0) read through. Quintilian, *Institutio Oratoria*, book 8, chapter 6, section 44, in Latin and in H. E. Butler’s English. Cicero’s ship: *Pro Sestio*, sections 45 to 46, found through Lewis and Short’s Latin dictionary under *navis*; Alcaeus: the note on this ode in the edition printed here. Auden: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 7.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: The word for *new* ends Horace’s first line and its noun, the waves, begins his second. The endings of the two words show that they belong together. Conington sets them side by side.
*Bravely seize.* The Latin dictionary of Lewis and Short cites the line under this verb, among Italy, cities, a mountain and a kingdom, each taken possession of. Conington’s ship is told to hurry.
The harbor comes first in Horace’s third line and ends his sentence. Conington puts it inside his second line, before the word that rhymes.
Horace says only *ship*. The adjective in front of it is Conington’s.
Horace asks the ship whether it does not see its own damage. Conington makes a statement of it.

lenses.caption: The English is John Conington’s, and it follows the Latin line for line. His preface asks of a translator some metrical likeness to the Latin. For this stanza he follows Milton’s version of another ode in the same measure, ten syllables for each long line and six for each short one, beginning off the beat as English verse usually does, and he adds rhyme. Auden wrote, of Greek, that unrhymed verse measured by length and rhymed verse measured by accent share only that both are patterns of rhythm. Latin endings let novi (new) close one line and its noun open the next. Conington sets the pair side by side, leaves out the question in Horace’s second line and adds luckless.
lenses.why: Conington’s stanza is his chosen stand-in for the Latin one; Latin ties adjective to noun by ending, English by position, so he joins what Horace sets a line apart; Auden says the two kinds have only rhythm in common.
lenses.stands: The two versions side by side, and the words tied between them. Conington’s reasons: the preface to his translation. Agreement of adjective and noun: Allen and Greenough, *New Latin Grammar*, section 286; the verb for seizing: Lewis and Short under *occupo*. Auden, on translating Greek: “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, pp. 5 and 6.

lenses.label: Order
lenses.name: synchysis
lenses.plain: the interlocked order: the adjective of one pair stands between the two words of another pair
lenses.caption: Each color joins words that belong together, as the Latin endings show. The verb, tore apart, waits a line for its object, the lands, with the Ocean named between. In the last two lines two pairs interlock: the adjective for the ships, the phrase for the waters, then the ships, the verb, the waters. Allen and Greenough’s Latin grammar calls this order a favorite of the poets. Its rule for any phrase, shown there from prose, is that the most significant word comes first. By that rule the weight is on impiae, impious, and tangenda, to be touched, with a not before it. Auden quotes the stanza for the older view that crossing the sea is rash, close to hubris.
lenses.why: Latin endings let Horace part adjective from noun; by the grammar’s rule, shown from prose, the first word of a phrase carries the weight, and here the words of blame come first, the judgment Auden quotes the stanza for.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. That each pair agrees in gender, number and case: Allen and Greenough, *New Latin Grammar*, section 286, with Lewis and Short’s entries for the words. The interlocked order and the place of the most significant word: the same grammar, section 598. Auden: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 9.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: The first word of the stanza and of its sentence. By a rule in Allen and Greenough’s Latin grammar, shown there from prose, the word most prominent in the speaker’s mind comes first.
The dictionary cites this line under a verb for tearing off or away, with the sense *torn asunder*.
A short form of *providens*, seeing ahead, and the edition printed here reads it so: foreseeing the evil to come. The dictionary calls that sense very rare and cites this line under *knowing, wise*.
The dictionary gives this line as its one example of the active sense, separating or dividing. In its other examples the word means *that cannot be joined*.
Without reverence for the gods, for parents or for country. The dictionary cites these ships for the word said of things.
A form of the verb *touch* that says what ought to be done, with a *not* before it. It agrees with the last word of the line. The dictionary cites these waters under touching as reaching a place.
Properly a raft of logs fastened together. In the poets it is any boat or ship.
Among the dictionary’s examples of things leapt across: the new walls Remus jumped in mockery of his brother, flames, nets, a river, and these waters.
Properly a shallow place or a ford. In the poets it is a body of water, the sea.

lenses.caption: The glosses are from Lewis and Short’s Latin dictionary. The stanza opens on nequicquam, to no purpose. The god is prudens, a short form of providens, seeing ahead; the dictionary puts this line under knowing, wise. The ships are impiae, without reverence for gods, parents or country, and the waters are not to be touched. The verb, transiliunt, means leap across: its other objects in the dictionary are walls, flames, nets and a river. The edition printed here finds in the ode a lament for the presumption of mankind. Auden, quoting the stanza, calls the attempt to cross the sea rash and close to hubris. Elsewhere he explains hubris as the Greek tragic hero’s belief that he is a god.
lenses.why: The words that judge the crossing are in the Latin: to no purpose, without reverence, not to be touched. The edition finds in the ode a lament for human presumption, and Auden calls the attempt rash, close to hubris.
lenses.stands: Each gloss is from the entry for the word in Lewis and Short’s *Latin Dictionary* (1879). The form of *touch* and the rule for a first word: Allen and Greenough’s *New Latin Grammar*, sections 500 and 597. The reading of *prudens* as foreseeing and the summary of the ode: the notes of the edition printed here. Auden: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 9; *Forewords and Afterwords*, pp. 19 and 21.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: Horace’s first word means *to no purpose*. Conington keeps the phrase for the end of his line, where it rhymes.
*Foreseeing* or *knowing*, the god’s adjective, stands a verb and a line end away from him. Conington makes one phrase of the two, and its noun comes from the same Latin verb, to look ahead.
The lands, object of the verb that ends Horace’s first line. A whole line of the Latin stands between them. In Conington the object follows its verb at once.

The Ocean and its adjective, *dividing*. Conington’s note on his own two words gives a line of Matthew Arnold’s that has the same adjective for the sea. The English that Auden prints with the stanza has it too.
*Impious* is said of the ships, with two words and a line end between adjective and noun. Conington’s ships have no adjective of blame. His goes to their plunge.
Horace says what ought not to be done to the waters: they are not to be touched. Conington’s one word says what they are.
*Leap across.* Conington’s verb comes from the Latin for stepping across, and its first English sense was *to sin*. It is his last word. Horace ends on the waters.

lenses.caption: Conington’s preface says he rhymed this ode in pairs, against his rule of alternate rhymes, so that readers might compare. In his English no adjective is parted from its noun: the god and his foresight make one phrase, the verb takes its object at once, and sacred stands next to its noun. Auden wrote, of Greek, that a language which marks its words by their endings does not need their order to carry the sense, as English does. The ships lose their adjective, and reckless goes to their plunge. For the leap Conington writes transgress, from the Latin for stepping across, which in English means breaking a law.
lenses.why: English shows by position what Latin shows by endings, as Auden says of Greek, so Conington joins what Horace parts; in doing it he moves the blame from the ships to their plunge and ends on a word for lawbreaking.
lenses.stands: The two versions and the ties between them. Conington’s rhymes and the line of Matthew Arnold’s: his preface and notes. Auden: “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 6; *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 9, where the English printed with the stanza is C. E. Bennett’s Loeb version, two words changed. *Transgress*, *providence*: the Online Etymology Dictionary; the Latin: Lewis and Short; Allen and Greenough, sections 286 and 500.

lenses.label: Contrast
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build
lenses.caption: Two sentences stand against each other. A strong breeze lifts the swan of Dirce, the Greek poet Pindar, whenever he makes for the high tracts of cloud. Nearly in Horace’s order: Ego, I, in the way of a bee that gathers thyme through labor, around the grove and banks of wet Tibur (now Tivoli), small, shape laborious songs. The swan is lifted and the bee works. Multa, much, is said of the breeze, and parvus, small, of the speaker. The edition printed here reads the ode as declining a poem in Pindar’s manner. Auden’s poem “The Horatians,” as Edward Mendelson quotes its close, also sets its speakers beside Pindar: they count themselves small makers, however polished.
lenses.why: Horace declines to write like Pindar by setting himself against him: a strong breeze lifts the swan, while he, small, works like a bee at songs that cost trouble; Auden’s Horatians, as Mendelson quotes them, call themselves small beside Pindar.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage and the two sentences themselves, with Lewis and Short’s dictionary for the words; antithesis as Allen and Greenough (section 641) and *Silva Rhetoricae* define it. Pindar as the swan, and the ode as a refusal: the notes of the edition printed here. The close of Auden’s “The Horatians” (in *City Without Walls*, 1969) as quoted in Edward Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden* (2017), pp. 778–79.

lenses.label: Measure
lenses.meterName: the Sapphic stanza: long and short syllables in a fixed order, three lines of eleven and one of five
lenses.caption: Dashes mark long syllables, curves short ones, dots the accents of words. This is the Sapphic stanza, named for Sappho of Lesbos: three lines of eleven syllables and one of five. Each long line here has a word-end after its fifth syllable. In the third line the swan’s sentence stops at that break; the next word is ego, I, whose last syllable runs into the next word. The new sentence crosses the short line and the stanza end, and keeps its verb, fingo, I shape, for the last word of the next stanza. Earlier the ode says that in his dithyrambs, songs for Bacchus, Pindar is carried along in measures freed from law. It keeps this one stanza fifteen times.
lenses.why: The ode calls Pindar’s dithyrambs measures freed from law and itself keeps one stanza fifteen times; the swan’s sentence stops at a line’s fixed break, and the I begins there with its verb held to the stanza’s end.

points.say: The full stop comes after the fifth syllable. The sentence about the swan ends there, and the next word is *I*.
*Songs*, and then the verb, *I shape*. It is the twentieth word of the sentence that began with *I*.

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The Sapphic stanza, its break and its name: Allen and Greenough, *New Latin Grammar*, sections 12 and 626, and the “Introduction to the Metres” in the edition printed here. What the ode says of Pindar’s measures: [its third stanza](#/read/horace-la/o4-02:2), with Lewis and Short under *numerus* and *solvo*.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: Both versions turn in the middle of the third line: a full stop, and then *I*.

The short line. Horace’s has five syllables and Conington’s four, which his preface says he chose to give its effect. Horace fills it with two nouns for manner joined by *and*, and Conington keeps a pair.
*Of Dirce*, a spring near Thebes, where Pindar was born. The swan of Dirce is Pindar. Neither version names him in these lines.
*Of Mount Matinus*, in Apulia. Horace was born at Venusia, on the border of Apulia.
*Plucking*: the verb for picking flowers and fruit, and for bees gathering. In *Odes* I.11 its object is the day, and there the dictionary glosses it *enjoy, make use of*.
*Costing much trouble.* The edition printed here thinks the word may describe how nearly all the *Odes* were made.
*Small.* The word agrees with *I*, four lines back: it is the speaker who is small. Conington says it of his powers.
*I shape*: properly *to handle*, and Cicero uses the verb of nests and honeycombs. It is the last word of Horace’s sentence. Conington ends on the song.

lenses.caption: Conington’s preface gives his stand-in for the Sapphic stanza: three lines of eight syllables and a fourth of four, to give the effect of the short last line, with alternate rhymes. He counts twenty-eight English syllables against thirty-eight Latin ones, and says he was constantly obliged to leave out part of the Latin. Here the high tracts of the clouds become skies, the thyme is only sweets, and the grove and the wetness of Tibur are gone. He keeps the turn in the middle of the third line, the full stop and then I. Horace’s sentence ends on its verb, fingo, I shape. Conington moves the verb up a line.
lenses.why: By his own account Conington gave the Sapphic twenty-eight English syllables for thirty-eight Latin and had to leave things out; here he keeps the stanza’s shape and the turn in mid-line, and drops the detail of place.
lenses.stands: The two versions side by side, and the words tied between them. Conington’s reasons are his own, from the preface to his translation. The Latin words: Lewis and Short’s dictionary under each, and the notes of the edition printed here. The same verb with the day as its object: [*Odes* I.11](#/read/horace-la/o1-11:1).

lenses.label: Book

measures.shown here: the third passage, from Odes IV.2

measures.measure: Three lesser Asclepiadics and a Glyconic
Glyconic and lesser Asclepiadic by turns
measures.shown here: the second passage, from Odes I.3

measures.measure: Two lesser Asclepiadics, a Pherecratic and a Glyconic
measures.shown here: the first passage, from Odes I.14

spoken of.as: where Horace says what he will be known for

lenses.caption: The Odes are 103 poems in thirteen measures. Thirty-seven are in the Alcaic stanza and twenty-five in the Sapphic: sixty-two of the 103 in two stanzas named for Alcaeus and Sappho, Greek poets of Lesbos. Thirty-four are in the five stanzas called Asclepiadic, the odes of the first two passages here among them. Seven odes share the other six measures. In the last ode of his third book Horace says what he will be known for: that he first brought Aeolian song over to Italian measures. The edition printed here takes Aeolian song to mean Alcaeus and Sappho, his chief models. Edward Mendelson writes that Auden shaped Horatian stanzas in English by counting syllables, as in his elegy for Freud.
lenses.why: Sixty-two of the 103 odes are in the two stanzas named for poets of Lesbos, and Horace claims that he first brought their song into Italian measures; by Mendelson’s account Auden made Horatian stanzas in English by syllable count.
lenses.stands: Counted from the “Introduction to the Metres” and the index of metres in the edition printed here, which agree with Allen and Greenough’s *New Latin Grammar*, section 626, on every list it gives. Horace’s claim: [*Odes* III.30](#/read/horace-la/o3-30:3), with Lewis and Short under *princeps*, *Aeolius* and *deduco*. Auden’s syllabic Horatian stanzas: Edward Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden* (2017), p. 416.

auden.says: In *The Enchafèd Flood* Auden also says what the older writers put in the ship’s place. A society in its ordinary state is pictured as a City or a Garden, the places where people wish to be and should be. A voyage is then an evil that has to be accepted, a crossing of what divides. Odysseus and Jason do not sail for the sake of sailing: one wants only to get home, and the other is after the Golden Fleece, in a far country. A ship of state that takes to the high seas by choice stands for a state in disorder: he calls it the Ship of Fools.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 7–8

auden.says: Against this older view he sets what he calls the new notes of the Romantic attitude. He lists four. The first is that any man of feeling and honor wants to leave both land and city. The second is that the sea is where man really is, and that to be on a voyage is his true state. The book is about that later attitude. It quotes Horace twice, both times for the earlier one, which Auden for convenience calls the classic attitude.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 10 and 12–13

auden.says: Donald Pearce, who took the class in 1941, recalls going to see Auden about it that September, before the term began. Auden named some of the writers the course would take up, and Horace was the first name he gave.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), p. 133

auden.says: Writing with Chester Kallman about translating opera, Auden sets the two ways of measuring verse side by side. In verse measured by quantity, as Greek and Latin verse is, each syllable counts as long or as short, with a long counted as equal to two shorts. In verse measured by accent, as English and German verse is, the length of syllables is left out of account, and what tells them apart is whether they are accented. Music, the two authors say, measures in both ways at once.
auden.source: “Translating Opera Libretti” (written with Chester Kallman), in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 485

auden.says: Of Greek, not Latin, Auden wrote that poetry always loses a great deal when it is moved from one language to another, and that between two languages as distant as Greek and English one can nearly say that a version which succeeds as an English poem is by so much less like the Greek one. Unrhymed verse measured by length and rhymed verse measured by accent share only that both are patterns of rhythm. Greek, he adds, marks its words by their endings, so that its sense does not hang on where a word stands, as the sense of an English sentence does.
auden.source: “The Greeks and Us,” in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 5–6

auden.says: Edward Mendelson’s biography records that Auden took Marianne Moore’s way of counting syllables and shaped it into Horatian stanzas, first in the poem “Where do They come from?” and then in his elegy for Freud. It also records what Auden said to James Michie, a translator of Horace whom he admired, about his “Thanksgiving for a Habitat”: he had set out on purpose to write the poem Horace might write as a living poet whose first language was English. Of “River Profile,” a poem of 1966, Mendelson says that it is written in twelve Sapphic stanzas.
auden.source: Edward Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden: A Critical Biography* (2017), pp. 416, 747 and 773

auden.says: In the spring of 1968 Auden wrote “The Horatians,” a poem about people of Horace’s kind, among them, by Edward Mendelson’s account, country clergy, curators and writers of short poems. It ends with the creed they have learned from Horace: set beside Pindar as makers, and beside real martyrs such as Regulus as lives, they rank themselves low; all they can do is the work they are fitted for, taking a glad and sober view of the world. Mendelson calls this creed quietly self-satisfied, and says its speakers are wrong about Regulus in a way clear to Auden.
auden.source: “The Horatians” (written 1968; in *City Without Walls*, 1969), as described and quoted in Edward Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden: A Critical Biography* (2017), pp. 778–79

auden.says: At the end of an essay on Pope, Auden wrote that poetry is no escape from life, though it gives a short rest from the troubles of the moment. He adds that with age, and in darker and harder times, Horace and Pope are the kind of poet he goes back to more and more often for that rest.
auden.source: “A Civilized Voice,” in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 124

sources: The Latin text: *The Works of Horace, with English Notes*, by A. J. Macleane, revised and edited by Reginald H. Chase (Boston: Allyn and Bacon, 1895), as Project Gutenberg prints it (no. 46938). Its notes on *Odes* I.3, I.14, III.30 and IV.2 and its “Introduction to the Metres,” with the index of metres after it, are used here.

The English: John Conington, *The Odes and Carmen Saeculare of Horace, Translated into English Verse* (first published in 1863), the third edition (London: Bell and Daldy, 1865), as Project Gutenberg prints it (no. 5432), with his preface and his note on *Odes* I.3.

Other places in the same Latin text: the whole of [*Odes* I.14](#/read/horace-la/o1-14:0), the third stanza of [*Odes* IV.2](#/read/horace-la/o4-02:2), [*Odes* I.11](#/read/horace-la/o1-11:1) and [*Odes* III.30](#/read/horace-la/o3-30:3).
W. H. Auden, *The Enchafèd Flood, or The Romantic Iconography of the Sea* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 6–10 and 12–13.

Horace, *The Odes and Epodes*, with an English translation by C. E. Bennett (Loeb Classical Library; first published 1914), in a later printing at the Internet Archive: the edition named on Auden’s reading list, compared here for the two places he quotes and for the third passage.
W. H. Auden, *The Dyer’s Hand and Other Essays* (1962): “Translating Opera Libretti,” written with Chester Kallman, p. 485.
W. H. Auden, *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973): “The Greeks and Us,” pp. 5–6, 19 and 21; “A Civilized Voice,” p. 124.
W. H. Auden, “The Horatians” (written in 1968; in *City Without Walls*, 1969): not seen in full; its close as quoted by Edward Mendelson.
Edward Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden: A Critical Biography* (Princeton University Press, 2017), pp. 416, 747, 773 and 778–79.
Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), p. 133.

Charlton T. Lewis and Charles Short, *A Latin Dictionary* (Oxford, 1879), at the Perseus Digital Library: the entry for each Latin word glossed, among them navis, fluctus, portus, occupo, nequiquam, abscindo, prudens, dissociabilis, impius, tango, ratis, transilio, vadum, Dirce, cycnus, Matinus, Venusia, carpo, multus, nemus, operosus, parvus, fingo, mos, modus, numerus, solvo, princeps, Aeolius and deduco.

Allen and Greenough’s *New Latin Grammar* (Boston: Ginn, 1903), at the Perseus Digital Library: sections 12 (the accent), 110 and 286 (adjectives and their agreement), 500 (the form of the verb for what ought to be done), 595 to 598 (the order of words), 607, 608 and 611 (long and short syllables, the beat, the break in a line), 625 and 626 (the lyric lines and stanzas of Horace), and 641 (the names of figures; this section at Dickinson College Commentaries).

Quintilian, *Institutio Oratoria*, book 8, chapter 6, section 44: the Latin at The Latin Library; the English of H. E. Butler (Loeb Classical Library, 1920–22) at LacusCurtius, with Butler’s introduction.

Cicero, *Pro Sestio*, sections 45–46 (the ship of the commonwealth): the Latin at The Latin Library, found through Lewis and Short under *navis*. His uses of *fingo* for nests and honeycombs are known here only from Lewis and Short’s citations under *fingo*.
Online Etymology Dictionary: transgress, providence, prudent.
caveats: The dots mark the accent each Latin word has in speech, by the rule in Allen and Greenough’s grammar; words of one syllable are marked as one reader would say them. That grammar also teaches a beat of the voice within each foot, which is not drawn here.

Auden’s remarks on verse measured by length, on what translation loses and on languages that mark words by their endings were made of Greek, or of Greek and Latin together. He did not make them about these lines.

What is said here of Auden’s poems “The Horatians” and “River Profile,” of his elegy for Freud and of his remark to James Michie comes from Edward Mendelson’s biography; the poems were not read whole. Mendelson calls the creed that closes “The Horatians” quietly self-satisfied, its speakers wrong about Regulus.

In the third passage *plurimum*, very much, is left unmarked. The edition printed here takes it with the word for labor; the translator of the Loeb edition takes it with the grove, and puts the grove and the banks with the bee’s gathering, where Conington puts them with the speaker.

The Latin here is a school edition of 1895, the English a translation of 1863 as printed in 1865. Auden’s reading list names the Loeb edition, and his quotations follow its Latin: in line two of the first passage it has an exclamation mark, not the question mark printed here.
